metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening when Claude 'has' a client-comms-log skill: it isn't remembering your clients. It was handed a file of instructions. Client-comms-log names one such file. Let's crack it open.

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has a client-comms-log skill' out loud and the machinery you picture is memory — a running record of every client, kept across every conversation. That's the natural read. It's the wrong one.

Nothing gets stored between runs. Delete the skill's folder and Claude forgets no clients — there were none to forget in the first place. What stops is one routine: the logging steps that folder was carrying.

Here's what a skill actually is: one file. Client-comms-log is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions for turning a call or an email into a structured log entry. Claude reads it before it starts.
The machinery is boring on purpose: Claude reads the file top to bottom, then works the steps in the order they're written. No branching, unless the file itself says branch.

So the design choice is: a skill is a specification, not a memory. Payoff — the same log structure on every entry: date, contact, channel, summary. Cost — anything outside those written steps, and Claude is off the map.

So client-comms-log never handed Claude a memory of your clients. What it guarantees is smaller and more useful: every run, Claude reads the same file and produces the same log structure. That's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: Watch Claude produce a clean log entry and you haven't proven it understood the call — a file can be followed to the letter on a conversation nobody really grasped. Watch it produce a messy one and you haven't proven the skill is broken — it may just be a call the file's structure doesn't fit.
So: a skill doesn't give Claude a memory of your clients. It's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, engineered so every log entry comes out with the same structure, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one record you create the same shape every time — client call notes, deal-review memos, weekly status updates — and have it write you a SKILL dot M-D for that record, plain-language numbered steps, then read it back and walk you through exactly what it'll do, before it does anything. Go deeper: ask the same model to name the parts of the workflow the file can't capture — the judgment calls that would still need you — and to show where in the file it silently assumes you've already made them.

Write me a SKILL.md for it in plain-language, numbered steps I can hand to Claude, then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll do with it, step by step, before you do anything.
